title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
goal: Separate the owner from the view and choose when a span is safe to create.

prerequisites.text: Modules 1–2: expressions, comparisons, types, references, and checked cin.
Follow the prerequisite links: cpp.functions-contracts. New constructs are introduced before the assignment.

sections.title: Why three types exist
paragraphs: The same sum can be computed from three storage types. The owner changes, while the function needs only the start and number of elements.

std::array<int,3> is an object containing three ints with its size encoded in the type. std::vector<int> owns a sequence whose size can change. std::span<const int> is a non-owning view of existing ints and their count.

Angle brackets supply arguments to a library template: the element type and, for array, the extent. You do not need to author a template yet. Include <array>, <vector>, and <span> for their corresponding names.

sections.title: Size is not capacity
paragraphs: vector.size() counts existing elements; capacity() counts how many can fit without reallocation. reserve(10) provides capacity but leaves size at zero. After reserve, v[0] is invalid until push_back or resize has created that element.

push_back(value) appends an element; empty() tests size()==0. Teaching programs bound the sequence to at most 100 values. In an exception-disabled environment, allocation failure is not promised to be catchable; do not use it as normal input validation.
After reserve(10) there is storage but zero elements. values[0] becomes valid after push_back(7), when size() returns 1.

sections.title: reserve does not create elements
paragraphs: Check size after reserve and after push_back. Printing capacity >= 10 avoids assuming an exact capacity.

sections.title: Traversal and auto
paragraphs: for(int value : values) obtains a copy of each element. for(const auto& value : values) reads without copying; auto deduces a static type and is not dynamic typing. Mutating elements requires a non-const auto& reference.

Use an index when position matters. Compare it with size() and avoid subtracting one from a zero unsigned size. Prove !empty() before accessing the last element; front and back also require a nonempty container.
When summing, auto value copies the current small value. For reading a costly record use const auto&, and for modifying use auto& when mutation is allowed.

sections.title: span passes a range
paragraphs: sum(std::span<const int> values) accepts a read-only range. Compatible arrays, vectors, and built-in arrays can supply it. Inside, size(), empty(), [], and range-for are available; the function does not own the elements’ memory.

An empty span is valid when the algorithm handles it. In C++20 these types’ operator[] is not input validation: the index must be below size(). Do not execute out-of-bounds accesses as demonstrations; identify the violated precondition on paper.
The example’s span<const int> accepts an array, a vector and a raw array. The function does not take ownership of any of them.

sections.title: One function, three owners
paragraphs: Match the four sum calls to their inputs. Identify the owner in each call.

reveal.title: Reveal output and trace execution
paragraphs: The output 6 9 13 0 follows call order. The view inside sum exists only for the call.

tables.caption: Trace for this run
rows: The same function reads a different range.

sections.title: View lifetime
paragraphs: The owner must remain alive throughout span use. When a growing vector reallocates, pointers, references, and spans into the old buffer become invalid. reserve may reduce reallocations but cannot replace a lifetime argument.

Finish modifying a container before creating a short-lived span, then process it without resizing the owner. Do not retain a view into a local vector after its function returns. const in span<const int> restricts writes through the view but does not extend lifetime.
Create the view after filling the vector. If appending later relocates storage, the old view does not update. In this experiment read safely only after the vector is filled.

tables.caption: Vector owner and borrowed range
rows: v stores 4 and 5. No view exists yet.
v still owns the two elements. The view supplies a start and length 2.
v remains the owner, but element addresses can change. Stop using the old span.

sections.title: Choice and evidence
paragraphs: Use array for a small fixed set, vector for a dynamic count, and span for a viewing parameter. This separates storage from the algorithm. Linear summation needs O(n) time and O(1) additional memory regardless of the owner.

Test the same function with three owners and an empty view. Separately record size before and after reserve and push_back. Next, compare these abstractions with a traditional array while preserving identical boundary rules.
Use array for three fixed coordinates, vector for a count read at runtime, and span at the function boundary. For an empty range the sum starts and ends at zero.

sections.title: Now try your own task
paragraphs: Now the count comes from input. Build the owner first, then pass its range to the function.
Sketch n = 0 and n = 3: who owns the data before and inside the call?

selfcheck.prompt: What line do the four sum calls print?
feedback: Yes. Each element contributes to its own range.
An empty scan leaves the sum at zero.
Those are the range lengths, but the outputs are sums.

selfcheck.prompt: What does reserve(10) change for an empty vector?
options: Capacity, but not the element count

selfcheck.feedback: A view does not extend its owner lifetime.
Capacity does not imply an element exists.

selfcheck.prompt: What may happen to a span after vector reallocation?
selfcheck.feedback: Create the view after resizing the owner.

selfcheck.prompt: What is needed to accept this lab?
options: Source, actual results, original tests, and a contract explanation
selfcheck.feedback: A progress flag is not evidence of independent mastery.

selfcheck.prompt: What goes wrong if you create a span on an empty vector after reserve(10) but before three push_back calls? How should the call see all three values?
selfcheck.feedback: Allocated storage and live elements differ. Sum only size() elements, with no accesses after reallocation.

practice.title: Fill a vector and pass a span
practice.task: Read n in 0…100 and n values in -1000…1000 into a vector. A span<const int> function computes the sum; print size and sum. Reject extra input as invalid.
criteria: Check 3 1 2 3, the empty range and a short input. Explain why reserve by itself does not change the result.
A view carries bounds but neither owns elements nor extends their lifetime.
Do not use a span after vector reallocation; create it after filling the vector.
Add two cases of your own, including a rejection if the interface allows one. Explain one boundary result.
Keep the source, exact input and observed output.
practice.hint: Allocated storage and live elements differ. Sum only size() elements, with no accesses after reallocation.

steps.action: Sketch n = 0 and n = 3: who owns the data before and inside the call?
steps.why: Choosing storage and choosing a function range are separate decisions.
steps.expected: The vector owns the data before and during the call; span specifies the range.

steps.action: Validate every value before appending. Create the view only after the last push_back.
steps.why: A view created before filling does not get the new length automatically.
steps.expected: The starter gives 3 0; passing the populated range and summing gives 3 6.

steps.action: Check 3 1 2 3, the empty range and a short input. Explain why reserve by itself does not change the result.
steps.why: An empty range and missing input require different results.
